LS-0001:
He was born and raised in a house in the Moharram Bek district of Alexandria, a large residential district that holds a distinctive position in the heart of the city. It is the first thing that greets anyone arriving from the desert road, and at the same time it sits in the middle of Alexandria, as if dividing the city into two halves: one to the left and one to the right.

From Moharram Bek the view stretches toward the sea at the Shatby area, while the entrances of the express road, Suez Canal Street and the railway line all meet there. The movement of the city and its different roads come together with the calm of Alexandria, especially in winter.

The district was not a single picture or one social class; it was a varied world, where middle-class areas sit beside villas and palaces and small old houses. That is the place that witnessed the birth and the first years of the story.
LS-0002:
Before he knew the meaning of music, and before any picture of the artistic world had formed in his mind, there was a sound that filled the house: the voice of his father, the composer Hamdy Raouf.

This sound did not come from a device or a recording; it was present in continuous rehearsals inside the home. His father would gather with his friends from among directors, writers, screenwriters and musicians, along with people of the various artistic professions, so the space of the house became a place through which the details of artistic work in all its forms passed.

And so the artistic world was present around him from the very beginning; it was not something distant waiting to be discovered, but part of everyday life inside his home.
LS-0003:
The show had already begun, and the audience sat in complete stillness, when he entered the theatre for the first time with his father.

The entrance was from the back of the hall, and he found himself facing a scene he was not used to: large numbers of people sitting in the dark with no one speaking, and opposite them people moving and acting on the stage.

The child could not take in the scene, so he tried to call out to his father: “Baba”... but he could not even finish the word.

In an instant, his father put his hand over his mouth and silenced him at once.

It was not merely stopping a child from speaking; behind it was a lesson that stayed present in his memory. Afterwards, his father made him understand that what happened was out of respect for the sanctity of the theatre.

That was the first lesson he learned about the theatre; a lesson that did not begin from the stage or acting or music, but from silence and respect.
LS-0004:
In the holiday between the third and fourth grades of primary school, the first signs of composing appeared in his life. He made a melody titled “El Shokr Kelma Arafha El Teir”; it was his first melodic experience.

When his father listened to it, he praised him greatly. But Ahmed heard something else that stayed lodged in his memory; he heard his father talking to his mother behind his back, telling her that he was truly gifted, but that he did not want to praise him too much so that he would not become conceited, and wanted him to stay always down to earth.

It was a moment that carried two sides of the father's relationship with his son: acknowledging the talent, and at the same time making sure early admiration did not turn into vanity.
LS-0005:
In 1994, the experience moved from the space of the first melody to a real children's theatre work titled “Qasr El Rabi'”.

The work included fourteen melodies and dance numbers, which Ahmed composed and arranged, while the direction was credited to Mohamed Abu Salah.

The cast of the play were children his own age at the time; children who grew up over the years, and most of whom now work in the artistic field. Among them is Karim Abdel Naeem, who later became a set designer and art director.

The story here was no longer just the experience of a child making a melody, but became participation in a complete theatre work, with its melodies, arrangements, cast and director.
LS-0006:
In Alexandria there is a place with a different distinctiveness: Kom El Dikka, that famous residential district that rises above the level of the city and is known as the plateau of Alexandria. From this place Sayed Darwish came and grew up, to become one of the most important symbols of Egyptian music.

And in this very place, the composer Hamdy Raouf had a well-known presence. His name was tied to holding the memorial concerts for Sayed Darwish, and he was a pioneer in presenting new melodies to the residents of the area during these celebrations.

The occasion was not merely a passing concert to commemorate an artist; Hamdy Raouf would turn the period of celebration into a full festival, in which Kom El Dikka lived an artistic atmosphere that extended across the place and its people.

Ahmed was still in primary school at the time. He does not remember the year exactly, but the picture of those celebrations remains part of the scene that surrounded his childhood, and of his father's artistic world that was present in the city.
LS-0007:
Music was not present in Ahmed's life through his father alone; it also had an extension within the family.

Mohamed Hamdy Raouf, his younger brother, became a music arranger and artist, and his name appeared in many works that carry his signature in arranging.

As for Amal Hamdy Raouf, his sister, she now works with him as an executive producer on most of his works.

And so the family story is not limited to blood ties alone; it extends to professional and artistic cooperation that brings the members of the family together, and gives each of them a place in the course of the work.
LS-0008:
The first musical instrument Ahmed learned was the piano, and his father was his first teacher.

His relationship with the instrument did not begin through an educational institution or a specialist teacher, but from inside the home, at the hands of Hamdy Raouf himself.

And so Ahmed's first steps in learning music were directly tied to his father; the father was not merely a composer whose works were heard in the house, but the first one who put his hand on the road of musical learning.
LS-0009:
From the second grade of primary school, Ahmed began a journey of music education parallel to his school studies, enrolling at the Conservatoire in Alexandria.

His first instrument of specialization was the clarinet, a wind instrument. But the road did not continue as it began; he developed a chest allergy in childhood, and was barred from playing the clarinet because of his health condition.

He had to move to another instrument, and so the double bass became his specialization.

It was not merely a change of musical instrument, but an early turning point in his musical study path; from a wind instrument to a string instrument of a different nature and style.
LS-0010:
In his teenage years, Ahmed played a different role at Victory College (EBS).

He was not there as a trainee or a student receiving singing and choir instruction; he was the voice and choir trainer.

This is an important point in the course of his formation; because it shows that his relationship with music was not based on learning alone, but began early to take on a teaching and training side as well.
LS-0011:
The beginning with professional singers did not come from nowhere; it was preceded by composing a large number of songs for singers from Alexandria. But among these experiences there was a different milestone: the first melody Ahmed gave to a professional singer.

The melody was for the singer Ali El Haggar, and it was called “El Midan”.

With this song, Ahmed's experience moved to a new space; it was no longer limited to early attempts and experiments, but there was now a melody linked to the name of one of the most prominent voices in Egyptian singing.

That was the beginning of a new stage in his relationship with the world of professionalism, and a milestone worth stopping at, because the first professional collaboration always remains a turning point in the career of any composer.
LS-0012:
Alexandria was the city that witnessed his birth, childhood and musical beginnings, but continuing the study path required moving to Cairo.

Ahmed moved to the capital to enrol at the Higher Institute of Arabic Music at the Academy of Arts, and continue his musical studies in a new stage of his life.

The move was not merely a change of the place of study; it was also the beginning of a different living experience. In the first years in Cairo, he lived in an apartment with his friends, far from the home where he grew up in Alexandria.

And so a new stage began, combining continuing his studies, independence in daily life, and dealing with a city different in its rhythm and challenges.
LS-0013:
The first wage Ahmed received in his life was for the melodies he made for the children's play “Qasr El Rabi'”.

The amount was relatively large for him at that time, and it was the first time he felt that what he offered in music could be work for which he was paid.

But his father Hamdy Raouf had a different view on how to deal with a first wage.

He told him that the first wage in life should be given as gifts to his mother and siblings. Ahmed took the advice seriously, and bought gifts for his mother and his two siblings Mohamed and Amal with the whole amount.

And after he did that, something happened that he did not expect.

His father returned the whole amount to him, and even added to it, then deposited it in the bank in his name.

It was not merely getting the money back; Ahmed's first reward became a family memory that stayed in his mind, and he himself described it as: “an event that will never be forgotten”.
LS-0014:
Ali El Haggar had been a familiar name in Ahmed's life since childhood; he knew him through his father Hamdy Raouf.

After the work on “El Sa'irun Niyaman” was finished, in which Hamdy Raouf composed and arranged 57 songs, Ali El Haggar heard a melody by Ahmed inside the studio.

At that time, Ali El Haggar had lyrics written by Nasser Rashwan about the 2011 revolution. The lyrics had been shown to a number of major composers, but the melodies offered for them did not please him.

El Haggar raised the matter with Ahmed, and asked whether he would like to try composing the lyrics.

His phrase at first stirred some apprehension; Ahmed laughed at the idea of trying lyrics that major composers had already dealt with, and described it as “the start of a worry”.

But he took the lyrics and began working on them.

There was a problem in the nature of the text itself; it was written as a poem, not as traditional song lyrics. So Ahmed did not treat it as ready-made song lyrics for composing, but came up with an idea for building the song and the way of presenting the text musically.

The result was acceptable to Ali El Haggar, and even won his admiration and affection.

And so “El Midan” became an important milestone at the start of the artistic collaboration between Ahmed and Ali El Haggar.
LS-0015:
The first years in Cairo were not easy, and the difficulty was not tied to being away from home or to study alone; there was a clear difference between what Ahmed wanted for himself and what his father saw as right for his future.

Ahmed wanted to work and get involved in the artistic field, like his friends who had begun their own practical experiences, while Hamdy Raouf saw that the priority at that stage should be study.

So his father forbade him from working during the first years in Cairo, and insisted that he focus on the Higher Institute of Arabic Music, and achieve high academic grades.

Ahmed found great difficulty in this; he saw opportunities and experiences happening around him and wanted to be part of them, while his father refused to let him be distracted from his study.

And the father would get angry if Ahmed went against this decision.

The original text indicates that many difficult situations happened because of this disagreement, and that their details can be told later. This is one of the stories that should not be shortened; because it reveals an important side of the relationship between father and son, between the desire for artistic take-off and the insistence on building the academic foundation first.
LS-0016:
The story of the song “Qalb Wahid” did not begin with the film it was later linked to; the melody existed three years before the film.

Ahmed had previously worked with the artist Medhat Saleh on the series “Haret El Za'faran”, whose melodies were composed by Hamdy Raouf, while Ahmed handled arranging the songs and the score.

Through this experience, an artistic acquaintance formed between Ahmed and Medhat Saleh, and there was room to present a new work bringing them together.

When the song was presented to the production side, the company had already chosen another singer to perform it. But Ahmed objected to this choice, and insisted that Medhat Saleh sing it.

The reply came that they would not be able to bring Medhat Saleh, but Ahmed did not back down, and told them: “Leave it to me, I'll talk to him”.

He took the matter on himself, called Medhat Saleh, and in the end Medhat sang the song.

That is how the story began of a song that would later become one of the important milestones in Ahmed's career, and behind the choice of its voice was a clear insistence that the song reach the singer he saw as right for it.
LS-0017:
In 1999, Ahmed entered the world of television at the age of fifteen.

The beginning was through two works composed by his father Hamdy Raouf: “El Shehab” and “Amsek El Khashab”.

In these two works, Ahmed handled the musical arrangement and the score, while the melodies were signed by his father.

His entry into television was not just a passing opportunity; it came through his father, who had placed great artistic trust in him since he was young.

And so, Ahmed found himself at an early age inside the television work environment, dealing with music as a real professional responsibility, not merely an educational experience or a hobby.
LS-0018:
The journey of musical study was not a single stage, but passed through two main stations.

Ahmed began his studies at the Arabic Music Institute in Alexandria, where he studied the secondary stage and the diploma.

Then he moved to Cairo to continue his studies at the Higher Institute of Arabic Music, part of the Academy of Arts, which is the stage equivalent to the bachelor's degree.

The move between the two institutes was an extension of a path that began early in Alexandria, but it opened before him a new level of study, specialization, and contact with musical life in the capital.
LS-0019:
During his studies at the Higher Institute of Arabic Music, there were a number of professors who represent important stations in Ahmed's scientific and musical formation.

Among the most prominent names he mentioned:

Dr. Alfred Gamil, may God have mercy on him.

Dr. Fathy El Khamissy.

Dr. Mohamed El Hedeiry.

Dr. Ahmed Youssef.

These names are part of the memory of the academic stage, but the value of the story is not limited to mentioning the professors' names; it extends to what each of them left as an effect on the way of thinking and dealing with music.
LS-0020:
The most important benefit of moving to Cairo was not limited to lectures or curricula; Cairo itself was a wide space of learning.

There, contact with musicians and artists became more intense, and Ahmed began to learn directly about the nature of work inside studios, with singers, and in theatre, video, series and cinema, as well as agreement sessions and professional dealings.

The difference was clear to him between Alexandria and Cairo; in Alexandria the volume of work and pressure was lower, while Cairo was the real centre of the artistic market, where works, opportunities and professional relationships intersect on a daily basis.

As for the institute, it played another role; it confirmed many pieces of information and experience that Ahmed already knew from his father.

And here a very important point in the story appears: despite the value of academic study, the professors and the experiences he went through, Ahmed saw that his father Hamdy Raouf was the most important institute and the most important teacher in his life, and that he taught him everything before anyone else.

This was not belittling the value of academic education, but a recognition of the standing of the first formation he received inside the home, at the hands of the father in whose life and work music was present every day.
LS-0021:
The years of study at the institute stretched over a long period, and the reason was not the difficulty of the study alone, but the artistic work that began to impose itself on Ahmed's life.

He was busy with works and professional commitments, so he missed exams, failed, and his years of study were postponed again and again. While his career was moving and advancing, the academic certificate remained postponed.

Until the year 2011 came, and he made the decision to finish this stage and obtain his certificate.

But reaching the end was not easy; it was a year full of pressures tied to finishing paperwork and completing procedures, and it coincided with the events of the 25 January 2011 revolution, and with his entry into the Egyptian Armed Forces.

Many files came together in a single year: the study whose completion had long been awaited, the political circumstances the country was going through, and the beginning of the military service stage.

And so the year 2011 became a milestone crowded with challenges and transformations in Ahmed's life.
LS-0022:
Since 2009, Ahmed began to take on the artistic management of the musical band of the artist Ali El Haggar.

The relationship was no longer limited to presenting a melody or a musical arrangement for a particular work, but turned into continuous professional cooperation, in which Ahmed became responsible for the artistic management of the band.

This relationship lasted for many years and continues to this day, becoming one of the most prominent long-running professional relationships in his career.

It is a relationship that began from musical work, then widened to include artistic responsibility and band management, and continued cooperation across different stages.
LS-0023:
Among the works whose reach and spread Ahmed clearly heard about was the song “Qalb Wahid”.

Its spread was not ordinary in his eyes; the song stayed present, and the positive reactions linked to it continued years after it appeared.

Ahmed felt proud of it, not only as an artistic work that succeeded and spread, but because of the human stories connected to it.

Among these stories is that of two of his friends, each of whom met his wife because of the song.

One story was more particular: a girl who had not yet met her fiancé asked him to send her the song's ringtone on her phone, at a time when phones used song tones as ringtones.

And so “Qalb Wahid” left the limits of recording and listening, and became part of the memories and personal experiences in the lives of real people.

Perhaps this was one of the meanings that made Ahmed remain proud of the song to this day: that the melody did not stay inside the artwork, but found its way into people's lives.
LS-0024:
Ahmed's relationship with the National Theatre had begun in his childhood, through being there with his father Hamdy Raouf.

The name Hamdy Raouf was well known on the National Theatre's posters, and it appeared repeatedly tied to the works he presented there. So the National Theatre was not merely a workplace for Ahmed, but a space that carried a personal and artistic history tied to his father.

Then came the play “El Ma'agana” in 2018, which witnessed a completely different moment.

For the first time, Ahmed's name was written on the National Theatre poster before the name of Hamdy Raouf.

It may seem a detail in the order of names, but it was not so for him. He felt a great burden and responsibility; the place where he was used to seeing his father's name now put his own name first.

And there was another thing that accompanied him in every work: that he always anticipates his father's opinion of what he presents, as if the father's presence and judgement were still part of the work process itself.

This gains greater importance when we remember the standing the National Theatre holds in Egyptian and Arab theatre; it is, as Ahmed describes it, one of the most important theatres in the Middle East and the Arab world.
LS-0025:
In 2025, the company Panther Art was founded in Egypt.

It was founded as a company specialized in artistic production, training in the performing arts, and intellectual property rights.

With this step, Ahmed's accumulated experience in music, production, artistic work and training moved into an institutional framework that carries the name of his company, and brings these fields together under one entity.
LS-0026:
The UAE was present in Ahmed's life through repeated trips; he used to travel there almost every year, for different reasons, and this continued until 2023.

The UAE was not a passing stop on his life's path, but a place whose presence recurred over successive years, and became part of the map of his movements and experience.

But the original record does not specify the reasons for each trip, the cities he visited, or the nature of the works linked to them; so these details remain part of the story that we need to complete.
LS-0027:
There are artworks that are tied not only to their maker, but to the place they were born for and the message they carry.

Among these works is the Sharjah song “Al Sharjah – Khalli El Salam Wasel”, tied to the Emirate of Sharjah and His Highness Sheikh Sultan Al Qasimi.

The work carries the number W-0024 in the works archive, and its year of production has been settled as 2022.

And here there is an important documentation note: the year had first been given as 2023, then Ahmed corrected the information and confirmed that the correct year is 2022, on 8 November 2026.

And so 2022 became the adopted date in telling this station.
LS-0028:
In 2025, Ahmed received the Golden Residency in the United Arab Emirates under the category of artists and creatives.

This station represents official recognition of his artistic and creative standing, and adds an important mark to his path and his relationship with the UAE.

But the story does not stop at the date of obtaining the residency; there are details worth documenting about the nomination, the application, the procedures, and the moment he learned of the acceptance.
LS-0029:
In late 2006, an important station began in Ahmed's training path, when he was commissioned to train the National Children's Songs Troupe.

The choirs and the National Children's Songs Troupe were affiliated with the Ministry of Culture, and the commissioning, the contracting and the creation of the troupe came through the then head of the General Authority for Cultural Palaces, the artist Ahmed Nawar.

This was not merely taking part in training a choir; there was an official commission to create the troupe and train it, so that a new experience began of working with children's voices and forming a singing group with its own identity and nature of work.

This station shows that the training side of Ahmed's career began early, many years before founding his company.
LS-0030:
Before Panther Art became a legal entity in 2025, Ahmed had already built practical experience in training choirs and preparing voices for artistic works.

Among the works recorded using this choir are “Wesh El Kheir” and “Mostaqbalna Ma'ak”.

The important point here is that the choir used in recording the two works is the same choir that Ahmed was training.

Therefore these works are attributed to Ahmed in the period before the company was founded as a legal entity, and should not be attributed retroactively to Panther Art merely because the company later became the institutional framework of his artistic activity.

This is a very important point in documenting ownership and professional history: the activity, the work and the experience preceded the founding of the legal entity.
LS-0031:
Between August and October of 2026, Ahmed was in the United Arab Emirates, busy coordinating other artistic works, when he received a call from the producing company and his friend the director Mohamed Zaki.

The talk was about a new theatre project named “Feen Albi?”, which revives the world of the great artist Mohamed Fawzi.

What was required was not merely preparing a set of songs for the theatre, but building a complete musical world for the show.

It was agreed by phone that Ahmed would set the artistic and musical vision, and present new arrangements of Mohamed Fawzi's songs, in addition to cleaning, filtering and organizing the old recordings, composing new melodies and songs, and writing a complete score that treats the play as a dramatic work.

Execution began while Ahmed was still in the UAE, and he completed about half of the work there.

Then he moved to Cairo to complete the remaining tasks and recordings, and the work continued until 4 November 2026.

The next day, 5 November, the show opened, followed by the shows of 6 and 7 November, then the shows of Thursday, Friday and Saturday of the following week, at the Mövenpick theatre in Media Production City.

The play's songs were all in the voice of Mohamed Fawzi, while the closing song was in the voice of Ahmed himself.

During this experience, Mohamed Youssef was his artistic assistant, and also shared with him in training the voices.

And so the show went out to the audience after a musical production journey that stretched between the UAE and Cairo, and combined preserving Mohamed Fawzi's original recordings with making new music for the show.
LS-0032:
In 2022, a call came to Ahmed from Dr. Ashraf Zaki, inviting him to take part in a new theatre show.

He told him that he wanted them to work together, and that Ahmed should be part of the show's team.

The project was the play “Ya Al'ab Ya Agles”, produced by Riyadh Season, with the participation of Benchmark and the General Entertainment Authority, under the supervision of Counsellor Turki Alalshikh, and the company Selah.

Work did begin, and Ahmed took on multiple musical and artistic responsibilities, including the score, the musical arrangement and the melodies of the songs, along with the complete musical and artistic vision of the show.

The lyrics were written by Tarek Ali, the choreography was by Mostafa Haggag, and the executive producer was Azouz Adel.

The leads were the artists Rogina and Ahmed Rizk, along with a group of other artists.

The experience combined the different elements of theatre; singing, choreography, music and drama, which made Ahmed's role extend beyond just composing the melodies.
LS-0033:
2015

The story began with only two lines.

On the morning of a day in 2015, the poet Ahmed Fayez wrote two lines of lyrics for a new song. And in the evening of the same day, he was invited to dinner at Ahmed Hamdy Raouf's.

During the visit, Ahmed asked him to let him hear something he had written.

Ahmed Fayez began to say the two lines, and he had not written anything else.

But what began with two lines did not end there.

The two sat in Ahmed's studio, and the work continued until the whole lyrics of the song were complete. At the same time, the melody was taking shape with the words, until there was a complete song.

Ahmed prepared a preliminary arrangement, recorded his voice as a vocal guide, then sent the recording to Mohamed Mounir in the month of April.

And the months passed without a reply.

April, then the following months, until November came.

Ahmed was returning from Alexandria on the desert road when he received a call from Mohamed Mounir.

Mounir told him he liked the song very much, and asked him to stop his car and send him its lyrics immediately.

Mounir was preparing to travel to Germany for three days, and promised that he would carry out the song with Ahmed's arrangement when he returned.

But while he was in Germany, he heard the song through Bassem Darwish and Sebastian Müller of the band Cairo Steps.

The two decided to prepare a musical arrangement of the song as a surprise for Mohamed Mounir.

And when Mounir returned, he listened to the execution Ahmed had presented, and approved the work after some minor modifications.

Then the recording phase began, spread over several countries: instruments were recorded in Madrid, others in Berlin, and other instruments in Egypt.

And in the final stage, Mohamed Mounir recorded his voice on the song.

And on 15 December 2015, “Ana Mennak Etalamt” was released, and achieved great success.

It was a journey that began with two lines on the tongue of a poet at a dinner gathering, then extended to studios in more than one country, and ended with the voice of Mohamed Mounir.
LS-0034:
2011–2012

The song “Fagr Biladi” did not begin in the form the audience later knew.

Ahmed had set a melody to completely different lyrics, before the artist Ali El Haggar listened to it.

El Haggar liked the melody, said it was very beautiful, and that he was thinking of turning it into a song for Egypt.

And from here a new journey began for the same melody.

Ali El Haggar nominated the poet Nasser Rashwan to write lyrics suited to the new idea, and the poet received the melody to write on it.

The song did not reach its final form on the first attempt; the lyrics and the melody went through successive modifications until the final version settled under the title “Fagr Biladi”.

After that, work began on the musical arrangement, then the team entered the studio to record the song.

As for the video clip, its idea and direction were by Hatem El Sayed.

The production was by El Haggar for Artistic Production, and Ali El Haggar assigned the work to the company Sout El Cairo for Marketing, Distribution and Broadcasting.

Then came another station in the song's journey; it was presented at a festival, and won the award for best video song, known as the “Video Clip Oscar”.

And so a melody that began with different lyrics turned into a national song, then into a filmed work that won an award.
LS-0035:
2022–2023

The start of the collaboration on the series “Teatro” came through a call from Dr. Ashraf Zaki and the director Raouf Abdel Aziz.

The idea was different from the usual form of television series; the project presents a series that contains theatre shows within it, that is, the theatre itself becomes part of the dramatic structure of the television work.

This form put Ahmed before an unconventional musical experience.

He had to deal with old melodies composed by major composers for theatre works, and present for them a musical vision suited to their appearance inside the series.

At the same time, he composed a large number of new melodies for the work, among them the end title song, in addition to writing the score.

As for the opening title song, it was composed by Mohamed Medhat.

And so the experience combined dealing with an existing theatrical musical heritage, and making new music and melodies for a television series whose structure relies on theatre.
LS-0036:
In 2018, Ahmed was in the UAE when he received a call from Youssef Ismail, then director of the National Theatre.

Youssef told him that the director Ahmed Ragab had tried to reach him and could not, and that there was a wish for him to take part in a new theatre show, written by Sameh Mehran, directed by Ahmed Ragab, with song lyrics by Tarek Ali.

Ahmed agreed with the director, read the text, then returned to Cairo to begin work. The task was not merely setting melodies for songs inside a show; they worked for a period on the text, and coordinated the various artistic works linked to the play.

And as the work neared completion, Ahmed put forward the idea that the closing song be in the voice of the artist Ali El Haggar, as a dedication.

The theatre director contacted Ali El Haggar, and El Haggar listened to the melody and expressed his agreement to sing it, and that was before he knew that Ahmed was the composer of the melody.

But El Haggar set a condition concerning ownership of the melody's rights.

And here a specific agreement was reached: Ahmed grants the National Theatre a permit to use the song inside the play, and after the play's run ends the closing song “Enta El Medad” passes to Ali El Haggar, while the rest of the songs remain the property of the play.

This was not merely a production detail; it is a story of particular importance in documenting artistic rights, and how a theatre work can include a separate agreement for one particular song.
LS-0037:
In the shadow of the events of the January 2011 revolution, or immediately after it, the story of a theatre show titled “Tazkara Lel Tahrir” began.

The idea was by the director Sameh Bassiouny, and the experience was tied to a period in which the country was living through great changes, and the theatre was a space for expression and interaction with what was happening.

This show had a special status; it was the first theatre show not produced by the Cairo Opera House, yet it was shown inside the Opera for several days.

That came at the request of the head of the House, after he watched the show and liked it.

And the effect of the experience was not limited to its usual audience; the idea also won the approval of another segment of the public.
LS-0038:
In 2017 and 2018, the story of an important artistic partnership began between Ahmed and the Port Said poet Tarek Ali.

Tarek was settled in Port Said, and Ahmed saw his talent, so he told him plainly: you are talented, come to Cairo and settle.

The two agreed, and Ahmed travelled to Port Said and brought Tarek with him to Cairo.

As soon as they arrived, Ahmed had an appointment with the director Bassem Qenawy, director of the play “Amr Takleef”. The work was still at the stage of agreeing on the idea and forming the team.

During the meeting, Ahmed asked the director whether they had a poet for the work, and he answered that he had not yet chosen a poet, and that Ahmed could choose whoever he saw as suitable.

The opportunity was present before them at that very moment.

Ahmed called Tarek Ali from the café, he came into the meeting, sat with the director, the agreement was made, then Tarek signed the contract.

That was the beginning of a collaboration that extended to many works between them. Tarek settled in Cairo, and right after that they worked together on “El Ma'agana” and other works.

As for “Amr Takleef” itself, it is about the martyrs and a military border area, and the struggle of the officers who were martyred in terrorist operations aimed at blowing up military areas.

So the story was not merely nominating a poet for a theatre work; it was also the beginning of a poet's move from his city to Cairo, and the beginning of a long creative partnership.
LS-0039:
A pivotal story that needs completion

Shortly after his father's death, Ahmed was settled in Alexandria. It was a difficult stage, during which he felt lost, and did not know how to continue his path without his father.

During that period, his friend the director Ahmed Shawky (Raouf) spoke to him, and offered him work in theatre through the General Authority for Cultural Palaces.

But Ahmed did not want to repeat a traditional theatre experience. He refused the offer in the form proposed, and said he did not want to work unless the two of them would go through a new artistic experience, building it together step by step, making use of the Authority's limited production resources.

The idea was for the experience to take the form of an operetta, a libretto or an opera.

And the search began for a suitable text. The first idea was to work on a faithfully translated text, until they arrived at Shakespeare's play “A Midsummer Night's Dream”.

But they faced a problem: the available translations were mostly in formal Arabic and literal, which was not suitable for the vision they wanted.

So they brought in their friend the writer, poet and English teacher Abdel Rahim Youssef, to work on transferring the text directly into Egyptian colloquial.

This stage took time and effort, while trying to preserve the fidelity and poetic character of the original text, and at the same time presenting it in an Egyptian language close to the audience. During the work, a large part of the text was set to music.

Then the stage of choosing the actors began; auditions were held, and they drew in young actors and artists from Alexandria.

The experience was different even in how the roles were distributed; the show was presented in a double-cast system, meaning that each day saw a different team, with two actors for each role, and some roles were shared by three actors.

The project grew until the number of actors exceeded 120, by Ahmed's estimate.

It was not merely a theatre show relying on recorded music; the singing was live on stage, and the actors themselves were the ones singing, and the songs were not pre-recorded.

To reach this result, each actor underwent training that lasted from six to nine months, including singing, acting, choreography, movement drama and movement in general.

The experience began with a preliminary show at Qasr El Tazawoq in Sidi Gaber, then came the opening and five public nights at the Lycée theatre, and after that the shows moved to the Port Said Culture Palace and the Matrouh Culture Palace.

The experience succeeded greatly, but it was not continued because of production circumstances.

Even so, Ahmed still sees that the work is fit to be staged today, if it is updated and developed.

This experience was one of the great stations in his life; not only because of the size of the project and its artistic nature, but because it came a short time after his father's passing.

Even while composing, Ahmed was always thinking: what would my father's opinion be if he listened to this melody?

And the show carried a dedication to the soul of his father, the artist Hamdy Raouf.

And so, Hamdy Raouf was present in this experience through memory and the dedication, and through that question that kept accompanying Ahmed while composing: would my father have liked what I am presenting?
LS-0040:
In 2009, a new theatre experience came, titled “Akher El Forsan”, directed by Amr Qabil, who contacted Ahmed to take part in the work.

The play was shown at the Floating Theatre, which belongs to the General Authority for Cultural Palaces, and its lead was the artist Roshdy El Shamy.

As for Ahmed, he was the composer of the show's music.

Although the information recorded about this experience is brief, it represents one of the stations of early theatre work, and deserves to be returned to with more details about the nature of the music and the circumstances that accompanied the show's production.
LS-0041:
In 2021 and 2023, the collaboration brought together Ahmed and the director Captain Ashraf Zaki in two separate theatre works, presented through the Academy of Arts and the Higher Institute of Theatrical Arts.

The first work was “El Masrah Wahashna”, shown in 2021 at the Nehad Selaiha Theatre.

Then came the experience “Nesa' Shakespeare” in 2023.

In both works, Ahmed's role was not limited to providing music; it extended to include training, setting the artistic and musical vision, composing, and the music.

And so the collaboration combined the creative side and the training side, in two different experiences under the leadership of the director Ashraf Zaki.
LS-0042:
In 2011, Ahmed went through an experience in musical comedy through the play “El Bodrum”, which is also known by an alternative name, “Afarit El Bodrum”.

The show was directed by Sameh Bassiouny, and was presented at the Hosabir theatre in downtown Cairo.

The leads included the artist Shams, the artist Amr Abdel Aziz, Dr. Samira Mohsen, and the artist Doaa Toeima, along with a large group of artists.

As for Ahmed, he composed the work.

It was an experience combining comedy and music, and is added to the series of theatre works through which Ahmed began building his experience in dealing with music as an essential part of the make-up of a theatre show.
LS-0043:
In 2014, Ahmed was nominated to work on the play “El Mokhatat” by the director Sameh Bassiouny, with whom he had previously collaborated on the play “El Bodrum”.

It was Sameh who nominated him to take on the melodies and music of the work.

At the same time, Ahmed was busy preparing the show “Helm Fi Leilet Nos El Seif” in Alexandria, which means that the “El Mokhatat” experience came in parallel with a large theatre project he was working on.

The singing in “El Mokhatat” was recorded, not performed live on stage.

But the recording was not merely asking the actors to go into the studio and sing; Ahmed trained them for a period, then the actors themselves recorded the voices that appeared in the show.

And here, once again, the nature of Ahmed's work in theatre appears: music and composing on one hand, and working on preparing the actors' voices on the other.
LS-0044:
In 2012, an artistic collaboration began between Ahmed and the director Bassem Qenawy through the play “El Habl”, which was presented at the Taliaa Theatre.

The relationship between them was not born of this work; Bassem had been a dear friend of Ahmed since the days of the institute.

And when he contacted him to work on the play, a new experience began between them, in which Ahmed took on the musical preparation.

This station was the beginning of a professional collaboration with an old friend, in which the relationship moved from the stage of study and personal acquaintance to shared theatre work.
LS-0045:
In the early theatre shows Ahmed worked on, there was a clear direction: that the actors themselves perform the songs with their own voices, instead of always relying on singers from outside the show.

This included a group of works, among them:

“Qasr El Rabi'”.

“Gebal El Hadid”.

“Ala El Zebaq”.

“Afarit Masr El Gedida”.

“Sous w Sousa”.

“Akher El Mataf”.

“Men El Obour Ela El Amal”.

The principle was that the actor sings with his own voice, because his voice is part of the character he presents on stage.

But this was not possible in every case; when there was a small character whose actor could not sing, Ahmed would bring in singers from outside the show, to perform the songs in the voice of the character.

In this way, singing was not merely a musical element added to the play, but was tied to the dramatic character itself, and to how it is presented to the audience.

This direction reveals an early interest in the relationship between acting performance and vocal performance, a relationship that later became a clear part of Ahmed's experience in musical and vocal training.
LS-0046:
1995

Ahmed was not a student at the Anwar El Sadat school in Alexandria, yet the work came to him from inside the school itself. The director Mohamed Ali was the one who contacted him directly, and asked him to write the music and melodies for the school play.

It was an early step in his career, in which the commission came to him through the director directly, not as a student of the school.
LS-0047:
1997

Ahmed was not a student at Alexandria University at the time, but that did not prevent the work from reaching him. The director Mohamed Morsy was the one who contacted him directly, to prepare the melodies of the show and its complete musical arrangement.

The task was not merely setting separate melodies; it included ten melodies, in addition to the complete musical arrangement of the show.
LS-0048:
1998

In 1998, a new theatre collaboration came to Ahmed through the director of the show, who contacted him directly to write the music of the play.

Ahmed was not then a student at the Faculty of Arts at Alexandria University; the commission came to him as a musician taking on the preparation of the show's music.

The director's name has not yet been recorded, but it is an important detail we need to recover so that the identity of the work and the documentation of its team are complete.
LS-0049:
2000

In 2000, the director Mohamed Mansour contacted Ahmed to work on the theatre show “Sous w Sousa wel Harb El Basous”.

Ahmed's singing contribution to the show was one song, which carries an opening line or name that he remembers in this form: “Lala wi Lala wi Lala wi Lala”.

And Ahmed adds another phrase linked to it: “Amleen Ala El Alam Regala”, but it is still not settled whether it is part of the song's name or a line from its lyrics.
LS-0050:
2003

In 2003, the director Hamdy Abbas contacted Ahmed to take part in the play “Akher El Mataf”.

Ahmed was then a student at the Higher Institute of Arabic Music, part of the Academy of Arts. And the irony is that the show was presented at the Higher Institute of Theatrical Arts, which is also one of the institutes of the same Academy.

And so Ahmed was a student at one institute, and at the same time taking part in a work presented inside another institute of the same academic institution.
LS-0051:
2013

In 2013, a new commission came to Ahmed through the director Amr Qabil, and through contact with the staff of the producing body, the Ministry of Youth and Sports.

The work was an operetta titled “Men El Obour Ela El Amal”, and it was shown at the Ministry of Youth and Sports theatre.
LS-0052:
2019–2023

“Dandana” did not begin under its known name from the first moment. The beginning was through two videos: “Waseflouly El Sabr” in 2019, then “3 Salamat” in 2020.

With time, the idea settled in Ahmed's mind, and he began to treat it as a project with its own identity, and chose for it the name “Mashrou' Dandana”.

As for the first official track within the Dandana series, it was “Ana Ghalban”, a song by Bahaa Sultan, dated 25 April 2023.
LS-0053:
A whole career

There are certain words that carry for Ahmed a meaning that goes beyond mere praise of his work.

When he hears someone say to him: “You're as good as your father”, or “Ibn El Wez Awam” (a duckling is born swimming), or “Bravo Ahmed, your father's son”, he feels proud.

And it is not limited to the artistic comparison; any approval of his father's work, or a kind mention of him, or a prayer for mercy upon him, is also among the moments Ahmed treasures.

For in these words, people's appreciation of what he himself presents meets their love and esteem for the man who came before him and left his mark on his life.
LS-0054:
2012

In 2012, Ahmed and his father the composer Hamdy Raouf came together in a theatre work named “Beram Beram”, directed by Mohamed Morsy.

The melodies were composed by Hamdy Raouf, while Ahmed handled the musical arrangement. The work was not all executed in the same way; most of the arrangements were recorded inside the studio, while the remaining part was performed with a live band on the stage.

The singing also had its particularity in this work; Ahmed sang with his father, and most of the songs were in Ahmed's voice, and the rest in the voice of Hamdy Raouf.

The show came on the occasion of the opening of the Beram El Tounsi Theatre in Alexandria in 2012, and the play's lyrics were all from the zajal poems of the poet Beram El Tounsi.

Press coverage confirms that the opening ceremony was held on 26 April 2012, in the presence of the Minister of Culture, and that the play's melodies were by the composer Hamdy Raouf.

But this work carries, in Ahmed's life story, a meaning greater than its artistic details; it was the last work he did with his father.
LS-0055:
11 May 2013

On 11 May 2013, the composer Hamdy Raouf passed away.

The passing was completely sudden and unexpected for Ahmed; his father, by his confirmation, did not suffer from any illness at all. He did not have diabetes or blood pressure or heart problems, and did not suffer from a chronic illness, but was in full health.

For this reason Ahmed rejects what was published in the press about his father having gone through a struggle with illness; this description, by his confirmation, does not reflect the truth of what happened.

For him it was not merely the loss of a dear person, but the departure of the father who was present at the roots of his artistic life, and in his musical and human formation, and whose relationship with him extended from the home and the first rehearsals to the stage, the studio and shared work.
LS-0056:
11 May 2013

Ahmed was with his father at the house of his paternal aunt, his father's sister. About an hour before the death, Hamdy Raouf began to feel tired, and his blood pressure began to drop.

In those moments, he said to Ahmed, Amal and their mother:

“Forgive me, I'm tired, but I'm trying not to give in to the tiredness.”

Then he turned to Amal and said to her:

“Amoula, forgive me, it looks like I'm going to give in.”

And he said to their mother: “Forgive me.”

As for Ahmed, he addressed to him short words, but they stayed present in his memory:

“Take care.”

His father repeated it eight times, and asked them to be witnesses.

After that he began to recite verses from the Holy Quran, and to repeat the declaration of faith more than eight times.

Ahmed recalls these moments in all their details, and sees in some of the coincidences tied to his father's life and passing signs of significance about his greatness as a human being and as an artist. Hamdy Raouf was born in 1952, the year linked to a revolution, and he passed away after a revolution. He also died in his sister's house, a coincidence Ahmed connects with Sayed Darwish, whom his father loved very much, and who also passed away in his sister's house.
LS-0057:
May 2013

In the days that followed the death of Hamdy Raouf, Ahmed's friend Mohamed Nabil stayed close to him.

After the death, Ahmed found papers on his father's desk written in his own hand. They were not complete texts or arranged words; they were scribbles, random letters and scattered words.

Hamdy Raouf was in the habit of writing with a pen during his phone calls, so the papers carried the traces of those moments when he wrote while talking.

Ahmed gathered these papers, and his friend Mohamed Nabil wrote the lyrics of a song for Ahmed about his father, inspired by those papers and the personal trace they carry.

But the song has remained, until now, without a melody.

Whenever Ahmed tries to begin composing it, he stops and weeps for the loss of his father, and has not been able to complete it.
LS-0058:
26 November 2025

On 26 November 2025, the troupe “Abtal Masr” took part in a singing segment within the concert of the artist Ali El Haggar at Sakia El Sawy.

The troupe, whose voice and singing training Ahmed handles, took part after Ali El Haggar hosted them in his concert, where the audience received them warmly.

The troupe belongs to the Mountain View Foundation for Community Development, in partnership with Panther Art.

It includes children and young people up to the age of 18, and their training is not limited to singing, but also includes acting and drawing.

The participation was an opportunity for these young people to appear before the audience at the concert of a major artist, within an experience that combines artistic training with taking part on stage.
LS-0059:
From childhood memories

One of the first and most important lessons Ahmed learned from his father, the composer Hamdy Raouf, was respect for the artwork.

Ahmed recalls an incident from his childhood, when he entered one of the theatres with his father from behind the audience. The hall was dark, and the audience was seated following the show.

Ahmed began to speak in a loud voice, and his father rebuked him and muffled his voice, explaining to him that it is not right to raise one's voice while an artwork is being presented on stage.

That was an early lesson in the meaning of respecting art and the place where it is presented, a lesson that stayed tied in Ahmed's memory to his father and to his first experiences inside the theatre.
LS-0060:
Hamdy Raouf's musical method

Among the most important things Ahmed noticed in his father while composing was his deep interest in the drama of speech, in the way a word is performed, and in the effect it can leave in different auditory cultures.

Hamdy Raouf did not treat the word as merely a text on which a melody is placed; he understood that a single word can carry a different auditory and emotional meaning from one people to another.

The same word may be received by the Egyptian listener in one way, while the Saudi, the Omani or the Iranian receives it in another.

From here came his interest in studying the music of peoples, and understanding the meanings of the maqams and melodic phrases among each musical people.

And this interest extended inside Egypt itself; Egypt for him is not one musical colour, but many varied worlds.

There is the music of the coastal cities, like Alexandria, and there is the music of the Bedouins and Arabs, which in turn is not one colour; Matrouh differs from Siwa, and Sinai differs between its south and its north. There is also the music of the Canal cities, Upper Egypt, and Nubia.

Each region has its musical nature, and its different way of receiving the meanings of melodic phrases.

And this is what Ahmed saw in his father's experience: that composing is not separate from understanding the word, the human being, and the culture to which the listener belongs.
LS-0061:
Hamdy Raouf did not begin composing by merely picking up the words and placing a musical phrase on them. He would repeat the lyrics of the song again and again, listen to them, and contemplate their meaning and performance, until he understood them well, then begin bringing the melody closer to the verbal performance of the expressive phrase.

He understood that music is not separate from the way a word is pronounced, and that the musical phrase should carry the expression that the words carry.

In earlier generations, there were multiple schools of composing; among them the melodic-ornamental school whose pioneer is considered to be Mohamed Abdel Wahab, and the expressive school whose pioneer is considered to be Sayed Darwish, the artist of the people. Hamdy Raouf leaned more toward the expressive school.

He played the oud and the piano, and the moments of composing were for him moments of special creativity.

Of everyone around him, Ahmed alone was the one his father allowed to attend those moments in which the new melody is born. So Ahmed accompanied him in them since childhood, and watched closely how the musical phrase takes shape from the first idea.

With the passing of the years, Ahmed's position within this experience changed. After being a child watching his father create, he came to attend mostly as a music arranger.

And Hamdy Raouf would explain to him his point of view on building the musical phrase, and why he chose to build it in this particular way. Then he began to ask him, as the arranger, to clarify his musical point of view and bring it out in the arrangement.

And he always stressed to him the importance of the arranger understanding the composer's intent: how he built the musical phrase, and why he chose this construction over others.
LS-0062:
“El Malek Howa El Malek” – Saadallah Wannous

Ahmed was about four years old when he watched the first melody take shape before him moment by moment.

It was the melody of the song “Itfi El Nour Ya Bahiya”, from the theatre work “El Malek Howa El Malek”, written by Saadallah Wannous, directed by Mourad Mounir, and starring Mohamed Mounir, Salah El Saadany, Fayza Kamal and others.

Ahmed remembers that moment clearly: his father was driving the car, and they were going along the street, and suddenly Hamdy Raouf began composing the first two phrases of the song.

At that age Ahmed was not able to take in everything this scene meant artistically, but he felt great pride in his father; he saw before him a cultured, respected and creative father.

Ahmed sees “El Malek Howa El Malek” as a very important station in the history of Egyptian theatre, and also in the history of his father's music.

And so his first clear memory of the birth of a new melody became tied to the image of his father driving the car, and beginning to shape music from the words in front of him.
LS-0063:
The television series – W-0064

The artistic relationship between Ahmed and his father Hamdy Raouf was developing over time; from a child following the composing sessions, to a musician sharing the work with his father.

One of the most important steps of this development came when Ahmed took on arranging a work of his father's for the first time.

The work was the television series “Amsek El Khashab”, the work recorded in the works archive under the number W-0064.

Hamdy Raouf was very happy with Ahmed's arrangements, but Ahmed would sometimes discover the extent of this pride from his father's talks with his friends, not from direct words addressed to him.

He would sometimes hear him from behind his back saying:

“Ahmed is gifted, but I don't like to tell him so he doesn't get a swollen head.”

That phrase carried the father's way of dealing with his son's talent; he sees his talent and values it, but does not want to exaggerate his praise so that he does not become conceited.

And so, Ahmed's first arrangement for his father was not merely an early professional experience, but also a moment of transition from the position of the son who learns to the position of the musician whose artistic ability the father trusts.
